**1. [NEWS] Rate whiplash — the buyer freeze script**

**Hook:** "Mortgage rates jumped 14 basis points in one weekend. Your buyers are asking if they should wait. Here's what to say."

**Angle:** The bond market drove the 30-year fixed from ~6.5% to 6.64% in one Saturday, with the 5/1 ARM up 49 basis points. Buyers are rattled. The agent reframe: rates are still lower than last year at this time — the real question isn't "6.7% vs. 5%," it's "this house now vs. this house gone in two weeks with rates still at 6.7%."

**Fits 30s?** One idea: the single reframe sentence that converts a rate-panicking buyer into a buyer who makes an offer.

**Why now:** Bond market story broke Saturday Aug 22, volatility continued Aug 23. This is the exact conversation agents are having this week with buyers who are freezing.

**Source:** https://finance.yahoo.com/personal-finance/mortgages/article/mortgage-and-refinance-interest-rates-today-saturday-august-22-2026-bond-market-sends-rates-scrambling-100000981.html (Aug 22, 2026)

**2. [NEWS] Affordability refugees — Chicago is a destination market**

**Hook:** "Your seller thinks their buyer is coming from down the street. Realtor.com says they're coming from California."

**Angle:** Realtor.com's End-of-Summer Housing Update drops today (Aug 24) alongside a Cross-Market Report documenting "affordability refugees" — buyers fleeing high-cost West and South markets and landing in tight Midwest inventory. Chicago held 6.3% YoY appreciation with only 2.6 months of supply. The agent with this in their listing pitch is speaking to a seller's self-interest in a new way.

**Fits 30s?** One idea: reframe the seller's mental model of who their buyer is — it's not local, it's national, and that changes what their house is worth to the market.

**Why now:** Realtor.com Cross-Market Report publishes today. Case-Shiller Tuesday will show ~1% YoY nationally, while Chicago outperformed. Midwest is named as the tight exception to national easing.

**Source:** https://finance.yahoo.com/real-estate/articles/housing-week-ahead-home-prices-080100643.html (Aug 24, 2026)

**3. [TAKE] Comment below is killing your reach** *(TAKE-003 — ALREADY SCRIPTED, ready to film)*

**Hook:** "Stop writing 'comment below' on your posts. It's the reason fewer people are seeing them."

**Angle:** Meta has classified explicit comment asks as engagement bait and reduced distribution on posts that use them since December 2017 — policy documented in the Meta Transparency Center and still enforced. Engagement coaching keeps selling comment count as the metric because it's easy to put on a slide. The fix is one edit: delete the ask, replace it with a sentence another agent would actually forward.

**Fits 30s?** One idea: the single caption edit that improves distribution on every post from here forward.

**Why now:** Monday take slot, hook family 9 (Swap/List) per the take schedule. Script is already built, no production delay.

**Bank entry:** "Ask for the comment." (Marketing and social)

**Who profits:** Engagement coaching that sells comment counts on a slide — the metric is trackable, which is why it persists, not because it drives business.

**Source:** Meta Transparency Center, Engagement Bait Policy; Meta announcement Dec 2017 (receipt verified 2026-08-18, see TAKE-003 Data Source block)

**4. [STAT] Buyer agent commissions went UP after the settlement**

**Hook:** "After the NAR settlement, the average buyer agent commission went up, not down. Here's why sellers need to hear this."

**Angle:** Counter-intuitive and defensible. The average buyer's-agent commission rose from 2.36% (Q3 2024) to 2.42% (Q3 2025) — the opposite of what most people expected. Why: sellers who refuse to offer buyer concessions shrink their buyer pool to cash buyers and buyers who can separately afford agent fees, a thin slice of the market. Most sellers still pay 2-2.5% because the math works against cutting it. The agent who explains this at a listing appointment wins the pricing and concession conversation.

**Fits 30s?** One idea: why refusing to pay buyer agent concessions doesn't save money — it costs offers.

**Why now:** NAR settlement affirmed by the Eighth Circuit Aug 19 — it's now settled law, the practice changes are permanent, and this counter-intuitive commission data is the whole story going forward.

**Source:** https://www.offerpad.com/articles/real-estate-commission-rates-2026/ (Q3 2025 data); RISMedia settlement coverage

**5. [STAT] First 14 days or nothing — the overpricing conversation**

**Hook:** "Your seller wants to price high and reduce later. Show them what week three looks like."

**Angle:** A listing's first two weeks get the overwhelming share of its total attention — new buyers with saved searches, active window-shoppers, agents flagging it for clients. A price reduction at week three doesn't restart the clock; it restarts at a discount with buyers who already scrolled past. In a market with only 2.6 months of supply (Illinois, June 2026), overpriced listings stand out immediately, and the window is shorter than it looks.

**Fits 30s?** One idea: why week three is too late — and the one sentence to say at the listing appointment to prevent it.

**Why now:** Inventory is tight in Chicago (active listings down 7.4% YoY, June 2026, Illinois Realtors). Low supply makes overpricing more visible, not less.

**Source:** Illinois Realtors, June 2026 market stats. **Note at build time:** the "first 14 days" attention claim is a bank entry marked `evidence: research` ("Price it high, you can always come down" — Prospecting section). Verify with a current days-on-market or price-reduction figure before drafting the receipt beat.

**6. [STAT] Stop asking cold leads "are you still looking?"**

**Hook:** "Don't ask a cold lead 'are you still looking.' That question is designed to let them off the phone."

**Angle:** "Are you still looking?" is a yes/no question with a built-in exit ramp — the answer is almost always no, and the conversation ends. The swap is the whole payload: ask something that presupposes they're still in the process and requires a real answer. "I'm keeping an eye on the [neighborhood] market — has your timeline or price range shifted at all?" creates a conversation instead of a door slam. The database every agent already owns is full of these leads.

**Fits 30s?** One idea: one question swap that converts a dead-database call into a real conversation.

**Why now:** Fall is when agents re-dial summer leads. The earlier in the week this runs, the more useful it is to their Monday morning routine.

**Source:** sacred-cows.md bank entry "Ask a cold lead if they're still looking" (Prospecting and follow-up). **Note at build time:** specific conversion-rate stat for "are you still looking" needs receipt verification. If a sourced number can't be found, build as a Value Giveaway instead of a take.
